title: Wolfbox
wikitext:
{{Short description|DI unit}}
The '''Wolfbox''' is the name for the original passive [[DI unit]], '''direct box''', or '''DI''' as invented in the late 1950s by Dr. Edward Wolfrum, PhD, alumnus engineer of [[Motown]], [[Golden World Records]], Terra-Shirma Studios, Metro-Audio Capstan Roller Remote recording, and [[United Sound Systems]] in [[Detroit|Detroit, Michigan]].<ref>[https://www.soul-source.co.uk/articles/soul-articles/ed-wolfrum-detroit-sound-r2445 Soul-Source: ''Ed Wolfrum - Detroit Sound'' by Moss, Rob in ''Soul News Past'', 17 Apr 2012]</ref><ref>[http://tqmrecordingco.com/united-sound-systems-detroit Ed Wolfrum interview on United Sound Systems, ''TQM Recording Co.'']</ref> Used by [[James Jamerson]], [[Dennis Coffey]], Bob Babbit and other [[The Funk Brothers]], the Wolfbox was a key component in the 1960s and 1970s sound of recorded music in the Motown/Detroit scene.

==Origin==
[[Image:WolfBox2.jpg|thumb|200px|right|A vintage Wolfbox]]
According to Wolfrum, the idea for the creation of the device originally came to him out of necessity, from "…Recording bands back then [early 1960s] and the fact that I simply couldn't afford microphones."<ref>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fp2i7ag3tFk Detroit Free Press, Brian Kaufman and Brian McCollum. ''Wolfbox'']</ref> It was at Detroit's [[WCHB|WEXL]] in 1962 that 16-year-old staff engineer Wolfrum incorporated his newly created passive direct interface box – later known at the "Wolfbox" – as an interface from the high-impedance output of church PA systems to the microphone input of broadcast audio mixers.

==Recent versions==
In 2013, a limited-edition run of 25 new Wolfboxes were designed, plotted, supervised & signed by Dr. Wolfrum,<ref>[http://www.audiographicservices.com/wolfbox.html Statement by Dr. Edward Wolfrum on Wolfbox]</ref> in a non-exclusive (unlicensed) agreement with Acme Audio Mfg. Company. Using NOS components and original A-11J and A-12J triad transformers sourced from vintage gear, these new versions found their way to such places as Nashville's Blackbird Studios, London's [[Abbey Road Studios|Abbey Road]], and to [[Blue Note Records]] President and bassist [[Don Was]].<ref>[http://cms.bassplayer.com/artists/1171/don-was-channels-sir-paul-mccartney/47948 Bass Player, July 19, 2014. Chris Jisi. ''Don Was Channels Sir Paul McCartney'']</ref> After the 25-unit production, Dr. Wolfrum ended his Acme collaboration<ref>[http://www.audiographicservices.com/wolfbox.html Statement by Dr. Edward Wolfrum on Wolfbox]</ref> and released his schematic of the Wolfbox in 2014 for free public non-commercial use.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20210205005632/http://www.audiographicservices.com/wolfboxv4.pdf Wolfbox Schematic]</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wolfrum |first=Ed |date=2014 |title=Wolfbox Story |url=http://www.audiographicservices.com/wolfbox.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112012911/http://www.audiographicservices.com/wolfbox.html |archive-date=2020-11-12 |access-date=2020-11-12 |website=Audio Graphic Services}}</ref>
Now Acme Audio Mfg. Co. produces "The Motown DI" which uses a new transformer inspired by the original OEM Triad transformers, and is a partial clone of a DI box used on a small number of recordings at Motown.

==Molybdenum and limited resources==
The original Wolfboxes relied on vintage A-11J and A-12J Triad transformers whose metal structure (i.e. '''Molybdenum''' composition) became regulated due to mining and manufacturing toxicity<ref>[http://www.dshs.state.tx.us/WorkArea/linkit.aspx?LinkIdentifier=id&ItemID=8589970015 What You Should Know About Molybdenum PDF, Texas Dept. of State Health Services]</ref> by OSHA<ref>[https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/idlh/moly-mo.html Molybdenum (soluble compounds, as Mo)]</ref> and EPA restrictions.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20000823044806/http://www.epa.gov/iris/subst/0425.htm Molybdenum (CASRN 7439-98-7)]</ref><ref>[http://environmentalchemistry.com/yogi/periodic/Mo.html#Regulatory Molybdenum Regulatory]</ref><ref>[https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0433.html NIOSH Chemical Hazards]</ref>
